title: Why Elliptic Curves — Group Law in Pictures

questions.question: In the usual elliptic-curve picture over the real numbers, what does negating a point P = (x, y) do?
options: It reflects P across the x-axis, giving (x, −y)
It reflects P across the y-axis, giving (−x, y)
It swaps coordinates, giving (y, x)
It sends P to the point at infinity for any (x, y)
questions.explanation: For short Weierstrass curves (char ≠ 2), the inverse of (x, y) is (x, −y). Geometrically it’s a reflection across the x-axis.

questions.question: Which statement best describes scalar multiplication k·G on an elliptic curve?
options: Multiply x and y by k: (k·x, k·y)
Add the point G to itself k times using the curve’s group operation
Raise coordinates to the k-th power: (x^k, y^k)
Hash the point G together with k to get a new point
questions.explanation: Scalar multiplication is repeated point addition: k·G = G + G + … + G (k times), implemented efficiently by double-and-add variants.

questions.question: What is the identity element for elliptic-curve point addition?
options: The point (0, 0) on the curve
The point at infinity, often written 𝒪
The point (1, 1) on the curve
Any point with y = 0
questions.explanation: Elliptic-curve groups include a special identity element called the point at infinity (𝒪). Adding 𝒪 leaves a point unchanged.

questions.question: In the chord-and-tangent picture, why does P + (−P) equal the identity 𝒪?
options: Because a vertical line through x = x(P) intersects the curve at P and −P, and the third intersection is defined to be 𝒪
Because P and −P have different x-coordinates that cancel out
Because the curve equation forces y(P) to be zero when adding inverses
Because (−P) is defined as 𝒪 for every point P
questions.explanation: A vertical line hits the curve at P and −P, and the group-law construction makes their sum the identity point at infinity.

questions.question: Why can we use the chord-and-tangent intuition even though cryptographic curves live over finite fields F_p?
options: Because crypto curves are secretly real-number curves stored with rounding
Because the same algebraic formulas derived from the picture define a valid group law over F_p
Because finite fields have an ordering, so you can draw the curve the same way
Because finite-field curves have no special cases like point doubling
questions.explanation: Crypto uses finite fields, but the group operation is defined by algebraic formulas (with modular inverses) that are the finite-field counterpart of the geometric construction.

questions.question: What is the core one-way-ish operation behind ECC public keys?
options: Given k and G, compute P = k·G quickly; given G and P, recovering k is believed hard (ECDLP)
Given x and y, compute x + y quickly; given x + y, recovering x and y is believed hard
Given two primes p and q, compute n = p·q quickly; given n, factoring is believed hard
Given a hash h, compute a message m quickly; given m, finding h is believed hard
questions.explanation: ECC revolves around scalar multiplication. It’s easy to compute P = k·G, but hard (for real curves) to recover k from (G, P): the elliptic-curve discrete log problem.

questions.question: Why must an implementation validate an untrusted elliptic-curve point received from the network?
options: To ensure it is on the correct curve (and usually in the correct subgroup), preventing invalid-curve and small-subgroup attacks
To ensure its x-coordinate is larger than its y-coordinate
To ensure it was generated from a small private key
To ensure it has y = 0 so inverses are easy to compute
questions.explanation: Accepting arbitrary points can break security. You typically check the point is on the intended curve and, when relevant, that it lies in the correct prime-order subgroup.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the usual motivation for elliptic curves in practice?
options: ECC gives comparable classical security with smaller key sizes than RSA for many security levels
ECC is secure because the curve equation is impossible to evaluate without floating-point math
ECC avoids all side-channel risks automatically because points are two-dimensional
ECC makes signatures unforgeable even if the nonce is reused
questions.explanation: ECC is attractive because it achieves strong classical security with compact keys and signatures, but it still requires careful constant-time and input-validation engineering.
